Topic: Wealth and generosity (wealth_and_generosity) — forced by request

--- Christianity — encouraged ---

Wealth as such is not condemned — the rich are charged to be humble, generous, and ready to distribute — but it is treated as spiritually hazardous and held under judgment.

      “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal: For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.”
      — Matthew 6:19–21 — The Holy Bible, King James Version, trans. the King James translators (1611)
      Context: From the Sermon on the Mount: accumulation is spiritually dangerous because the heart follows the treasure; the standing charter for Christian detachment from wealth.
  • A remembered saying of Jesus makes giving itself the greater blessing. [C2]
      “I have shewed you all things, how that so labouring ye ought to support the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he said, It is more blessed to give than to receive.”
      — Acts 20:35 — The Holy Bible, King James Version, trans. the King James translators (1611)
      Context: Paul's farewell at Miletus, preserving a saying of Jesus not found in the Gospels; giving is presented as blessing rather than loss.
  • The rich are not ordered to renounce but to distribute — wealth is a stewardship, not a possession. [C3]
      “Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy; That they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate;”
      — 1 Timothy 6:17–18 — The Holy Bible, King James Version, trans. the King James translators (1611)
      Context: Riches are not condemned outright here: the wealthy are charged to hold wealth without trust in it and to give readily — a counterweight to purely renunciant readings.
  Further reading:
      - Peter Brown, “Through the Eye of a Needle: Wealth, the Fall of Rome, and the Making of Christianity in the West” (2012) [book]

--- Islam — obligatory ---
Almsgiving in Islam is not charity from surplus but zakat — a fixed, obligatory purification of wealth ranked with prayer among the pillars. Beyond the obligation, piety is measured by giving what one loves, to kin, orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer; wealth withheld from these claims is impure, not merely ungenerous.
  • Righteousness is defined by concrete giving to the vulnerable alongside worship and the poor-due. [C4]
      “and giveth wealth, for love of Him, to kinsfolk and to orphans and the needy and the wayfarer and to those who ask, and to set slaves free; and observeth proper worship and payeth the poor-due.”
      — Qur'an 2:177 — The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, trans. Marmaduke Pickthall (1930)
      Context: From the 'righteousness is not turning your faces' verse: concrete giving to named categories of the vulnerable defines piety before ritual correctness.
  • Piety is unattained until one spends of what one loves, pushing generosity past comfort. [C5]
      “Ye will not attain unto piety until ye spend of that which ye love. And whatsoever ye spend, Allah is Aware thereof.”
      — Qur'an 3:92 — The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, trans. Marmaduke Pickthall (1930)
      Context: Piety is tied to giving what one loves, not surplus; alongside the obligatory zakat this makes generosity constitutive of righteousness, not supererogatory polish.
  Further reading:
      - Amy Singer, “Charity in Islamic Societies” (2008) [book]

--- Buddhism — encouraged ---
Dana — giving — is the first perfection and the layperson's foundational practice: fools alone do not praise liberality, and the wise rejoice in it. Wealth rightly earned is no evil in the early texts, but craving is, and contentment is called the best riches; generosity is the discipline that loosens grasping while sustaining the community of practice.
  • Liberality is praised as the wise man's joy and the path to blessing. [C6]
      “The uncharitable do not go to the world of the gods; fools only do not praise liberality; a wise man rejoices in liberality, and through it becomes blessed in the other world.”

      Context: Dana — giving — is the first of the perfections and the layperson's foundational practice; the verse ties liberality to wisdom and its refusal to folly.
  • Contentment as the best riches reframes what wealth is for. [C7]
      “Health is the greatest of gifts, contentedness the best riches; trust is the best of relationships, Nirvana the highest happiness.”
      — Dhp 204 — The Dhammapada, trans. F. Max Müller (1881)
      Context: Contentment is named the best wealth — the positive state whose absence envy is; the verse reorders goods by their contribution to peace.
  Further reading:
      - Peter Harvey, “An Introduction to Buddhist Ethics” (2000) [book]

--- Confucianism — context_dependent ---
Riches and honours are what men desire — the Analects concedes the appetite and moralizes the means: wealth not gotten in the proper way should not be held, and ill-gotten prosperity is a floating cloud. Contentment with coarse rice is modeled without being commanded. Generosity flows through role-duties — kin, guests, the people one governs — rather than an abstract command to give.
  • Joy with coarse rice and water, and unrighteous riches as floating cloud, model wealth's right weight. [C8]
      “The Master said, ‘With coarse rice to eat, with water to drink, and my bended arm for a pillow; — I have still joy in the midst of these things. Riches and honours acquired by unrighteousness, are to me as a floating cloud.’”
      — Analects VII.15 — The Analects of Confucius, trans. James Legge (1861)
      Context: Not wealth but wealth wrongly gotten is the floating cloud; the passage models contentment without renouncing prosperity as such.
  • The proper way governs both acquiring wealth and escaping poverty. [C9]
      “The Master said, ‘Riches and honours are what men desire. If it cannot be obtained in the proper way, they should not be held. Poverty and meanness are what men dislike. If it cannot be avoided in the proper way, they should not be avoided.’”
      — Analects IV.5 — The Analects of Confucius, trans. James Legge (1861)
      Context: Desire for wealth is conceded as human; the proper way governs both getting and escaping. Acquisition is moralized at the means, not the end.
  Further reading:
      - Michael Puett and Christine Gross-Loh, “The Path: What Chinese Philosophers Can Teach Us About the Good Life” (2016) [book]

--- Kantian deontology — obligatory ---
The prosperous man who shrugs 'what concern is it of mine?' fails the test: his maxim can be conceived as universal law but not willed as one, since he too will need others' help. Beneficence is therefore a real duty — imperfect, leaving latitude in whom and how much, but not whether. Kant adds a corrosive honesty: much charity flatters the giver while injustice upstream created the need; duty prefers justice to condescension.
  • The indifference maxim cannot be willed universally: the non-helper wills away help he will one day need. [C10]
      “A fourth, who is in prosperity, while he sees that others have to contend with great wretchedness and that he could help them, thinks: What concern is it of mine? Let everyone be as happy as Heaven pleases, or as he can make himself; I will take nothing from him nor even envy him, only I do not wish to contribute anything to his welfare or to his assistance in distress!”
      — Groundwork 4:423 — Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, trans. Thomas Kingsmill Abbott (1873)
      Context: The beneficence example: the prosperous non-helper's maxim can be conceived but not willed universally, since he too will someday need the love and sympathy of others. Beneficence is thus a duty, though a wide one.
  Further reading:
      - Barbara Herman, “The Practice of Moral Judgment” (1993) [book]

--- Virtue ethics — encouraged ---
Giving well is an excellence with its own name, liberality, and it is measured against the giver's means rather than the size of the sum. The liberal person gives to the right people, in the right amount, at the right moment and for the sake of what is fine, so a lavish gift made to impress misses the mark while a modest one may hit it. Both extremes are faults, but stinginess is judged the worse and the more entrenched, since most people are keener on getting than on parting with anything.
  • Right giving is fixed by recipient, amount, occasion and motive together; the sum by itself settles nothing. [C11]
      “Now virtuous actions are noble and done for the sake of the noble. Therefore the liberal man, like other virtuous men, will give for the sake of the noble, and rightly; for he will give to the right people, the right amounts, and at the right time, with all the other qualifications that accompany right giving.”
      — NE IV.1, 1120a24 — The Nicomachean Ethics, trans. W. D. Ross (1925)
      Context: The core of the account of liberality. What makes giving virtuous is the fit between recipient, amount, occasion and motive, so a large gift made carelessly or for display does not qualify.
  • The two extremes are not symmetrical — meanness is commoner and harder to cure than extravagance. [C12]
      “Meanness is both incurable (for old age and every disability is thought to make men mean) and more innate in men than prodigality; for most men are fonder of getting money than of giving.”
      — NE IV.1, 1121b13 — The Nicomachean Ethics, trans. W. D. Ross (1925)
      Context: Aristotle breaks his own symmetry here: the two extremes around liberality are not equally bad or equally common. The judgment shapes how the tradition weighs stinginess against extravagance.
  • Spending on a large scale is a further excellence of perception, and one available only to those who already have resources. [C13]
      “The magnificent man is like an artist; for he can see what is fitting and spend large sums tastefully.”
      — NE IV.2, 1122a34 — The Nicomachean Ethics, trans. W. D. Ross (1925)
      Context: Magnificence is the virtue of large-scale expenditure, distinct from liberality and available only to those with means. Aristotle treats good spending as a skill of perception, which is why he compares it to art.
  • Flourishing itself needs equipment, so possessions cannot be treated as morally weightless. [C14]
      “Yet evidently, as we said, it needs the external goods as well; for it is impossible, or not easy, to do noble acts without the proper equipment.”
      — NE I.8, 1099a33 — The Nicomachean Ethics, trans. W. D. Ross (1925)
      Context: Aristotle concedes that flourishing is not wholly insulated from fortune: friends, wealth and political power are instruments of noble action. The admission is what keeps his ethics from treating poverty as morally weightless.
  Note: The account is frankly addressed to a propertied audience: magnificence presupposes wealth, and a poor person can exhibit liberality only in miniature. Readers divide over whether that is an incidental feature of the original audience or a structural limit on an ethics built from the excellences of a leisured class.
  Further reading:
      - Julia Annas, “Intelligent Virtue” (2011) [book]
      - Howard J. Curzer, “Aristotle and the Virtues” (2012) [book]
